source.title: Polysemanticity and Capacity in Neural Networks

record.file_problem: none; the full post and comments are present, but the underlying paper is summarized rather than included in full.
record.tranche_reason: Reports results from an analytically tractable toy model and a capacity-allocation analysis that bear on superposition and polysemanticity, using a different model and analysis from the original Toy Models of Superposition.
record.gate_note: The post reports findings from the authors' own toy-model paper, including numerical replication of capacity curves, sparsity-related results, phase transitions, and geometry. It also mentions results from Elhage et al.; those cited results are not recorded as this study's own rows. Comments proposing experiments are not results.
record.test_reason: The post reports the authors' own analytical and numerical results from a different, tractable toy model. These cover capacity allocation, the sparsity–polysemanticity relation, phase transitions and feature geometry, and bear on V1 and V2 in toy networks. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors argue that polysemanticity arises when marginal returns to capacity diminish, and hypothesize a fundamental link between sparsity and diminishing returns. They say that if features are sparse and similar in importance, polysemanticity is optimal. They suspect the framework captures aspects of real networks, though large models are 'substantially messier'. They also call the work a side project of uncertain importance.
record.recipe_differences: The post describes an analytically tractable toy model, a capacity-allocation framework, and a loss decomposition; it does not report using the original study's method. The underlying paper is described as an arXiv paper.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature sparsity changes the reported polysemanticity outcome; the authors also say the examined models show qualitatively different levels of polysemanticity as sparsity changes.
record.peer_reviewed: Alignment Forum post; the underlying paper is described as an arXiv paper.
record.problems: The post gives no numerical values, uncertainty estimates, named models, or detailed phase-diagram settings. Its results are summaries of a separate paper rather than a full report of that paper's methods and evidence.
record.rows_left_out: No reported own-result findings bearing on the listed versions were left out. Cited results from Elhage et al. and suggestions in the comments were not treated as this study's results.

untested.parts: Near-orthogonality angles, exact feature/dimension counts and quantitative geometry beyond the 'block-semi-orthogonal' description.
Whether important features get dedicated dimensions in real networks. Importance is mentioned only as 'similar enough in importance'; no importance-ranked allocation result is reported.
Not tested. The post only notes polysemanticity can arise 'in some other situations' without results.

missing.what: Analytically derived phase diagram and explanation of sharp phase transitions: capacities hit 0 or 1, and the post says these resemble Elhage et al.'s transitions. Only indirectly captured via r4/r5.
missing.locator: Main post, paragraph on phase transitions and phase diagram

record.verdict_notes: Evidence is a blog summary of arXiv:2210.01892, with no numbers, so all verdicts rest on textual claims. Commenters reported errors in the paper's derivations, which the authors say they fixed; the commenter says these do not invalidate conclusions.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not give quantitative angles or establish how closely the directions approximate orthogonality; the exact feature and dimension counts are not stated.
The reported results are from toy models, not real neural networks; no concrete measure of feature importance or dedicated-dimension allocation in an LLM is reported.
The post does not test whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure.
No indirect evidence from LLM feature spread or dictionary recovery is reported.
The post does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
The post does not test whether the represented features are one-dimensional.

relationships.condition: Authors' analytically tractable toy model(s), varying feature sparsity
relationships.reason: Several results match V1's sparsity-dependent transition and regular geometry. Polysemanticity rises with sparsity in all models examined (r2). The loss decomposition favours superposition as sparsity rises (r3). There is none in the dense regime and it appears in the sparse regime (r4, r5). Features form block-semi-orthogonal structure (r6).
relationships.display_finding: Polysemanticity rose with sparsity in every model examined, and the loss decomposition favoured superposition as sparsity rose. Superposition was absent in the dense regime and present in the sparse one, and features formed block-semi-orthogonal structure.
